For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$.

This is the right-handed **cross product**. The displayed coordinates are those of the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), and inner products and norms are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $F=(F_0,\ldots,F_{n-1}):U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$ in the componentwise Euclidean sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. Then the **divergence** of $F$ is $\operatorname{div}F:=\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i$, the function $U\to\mathbb R$ whose value at $p$ is $\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i(p)$. The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], and the sum is the finite sum used throughout [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Since each $\partial_iF_i$ is continuous on $U$, so is $\operatorname{div}F$.

Now let $n=3$ and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^1$ on an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$. Following [[def-cross-product-in-r3]], write the three coordinates of a point and of a vector as $x,y,z$ rather than $0,1,2$, so that $F=(F_x,F_y,F_z)$ means $F=(F_0,F_1,F_2)$ and $\partial_x,\partial_y,\partial_z$ are $\partial_0,\partial_1,\partial_2$. With that naming, the **curl** of $F$ is $\operatorname{curl}F:=(\partial_yF_z-\partial_zF_y,\ \partial_zF_x-\partial_xF_z,\ \partial_xF_y-\partial_yF_x)$, a map $U\to\mathbb R^3$ each of whose coordinates is continuous on $U$. In this naming the divergence reads $\operatorname{div}F=\partial_xF_x+\partial_yF_y+\partial_zF_z$.

Both operators are defined pointwise from the first partial derivatives of the components, so no differentiability of $F$ beyond $C^1$ is used and no orientation or metric structure enters beyond the standard coordinates of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]. For a $C^1$ scalar function $f$ on $U$, the gradient $\nabla f=(\partial_0f,\ldots,\partial_{n-1}f)$ is that of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]; in the three-coordinate naming, $\nabla f=(\partial_xf,\partial_yf,\partial_zf)$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $a\in U$, $v\in\mathbb R^m$, and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. If the line map $t\mapsto f(a+tv)$ is defined near $0$, its derivative at $0$ is the **directional derivative**

$$D_vf(a):=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(a+tv)-f(a)}{t}.$$

For a standard basis vector $e_j$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), $D_{e_j}f(a)$ is the **$j$th partial derivative**, written $\partial_jf(a)$. These are ordinary vector-valued one-variable derivatives in the sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]].

If every partial derivative $\partial_jf_i(a)$ of $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ exists, the **Jacobian matrix** is $Jf(a)=(\partial_jf_i(a))_{i<n,j<m}$. For scalar-valued $f$, its **gradient** is

$$\nabla f(a):=(\partial_0f(a),\ldots,\partial_{m-1}f(a))\in\mathbb R^m,$$

with coordinates understood in the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]). The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A bijection $f:U\to V$ is a **$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $C^k$. For $k\ge1$, a **local $C^k$ diffeomorphism at $a\in U$** is a restriction $f|_P:P\to Q$ between open neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$ that is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism. At $k=1$ this agrees with [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: continuous first partial derivatives give the required total derivative by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], while continuity of the total derivative gives continuity of its matrix entries and hence of the first partial derivatives.

derivations.claim: The entries $Q_{ij}=F_iF_j-\tfrac12\delta_{ij}\langle F,F\rangle$ are sums of products of $C^1$ functions, hence $C^1$ on $U$ by [F3] and [F4], so both sides of the first identity are defined; moreover $\partial_j\langle F,F\rangle=\partial_j\sum_{l=1}^{3}F_lF_l=2\sum_{l=1}^{3}F_l\,\partial_jF_l$ by the product rule [F4].

For fixed $i$, $\sum_{j=1}^{3}\partial_jQ_{ij}=\sum_{j=1}^{3}\partial_j(F_iF_j)-\tfrac12\sum_{j=1}^{3}\delta_{ij}\partial_j\langle F,F\rangle=\sum_{j=1}^{3}\bigl(F_j\partial_jF_i+F_i\partial_jF_j\bigr)-\sum_{l=1}^{3}F_l\partial_iF_l=F_i\operatorname{div}F+\sum_{j=1}^{3}\bigl(F_j\partial_jF_i-F_j\partial_iF_j\bigr)$ by step 1.1, the product rule [F4] and the divergence formula [F2].

For a symmetric tensor and fixed $i$, the nine-term sum $\epsilon_{ijk}Q_{kj}$ vanishes: terms with $j=k$ have $\epsilon_{ijk}=0$, and for $j\ne k$ the pair $(j,k)$ and the pair $(k,j)$ contribute $\epsilon_{ijk}Q_{kj}+\epsilon_{ikj}Q_{jk}=\epsilon_{ijk}Q_{kj}-\epsilon_{ijk}Q_{kj}=0$, because $\epsilon$ changes sign under exchange of its last two indices and $Q$ is symmetric. This is the second claim.

The first coordinate of $F\times\operatorname{curl}F$ is, by [F1] and [F2], $F_2(\partial_1F_2-\partial_2F_1)-F_3(\partial_3F_1-\partial_1F_3)=F_2\partial_1F_2+F_3\partial_1F_3-F_2\partial_2F_1-F_3\partial_3F_1$; adding and subtracting $F_1\partial_1F_1$ shows that $-\bigl(F\times\operatorname{curl}F\bigr)_1=\sum_{j=1}^{3}\bigl(F_j\partial_jF_1-F_j\partial_1F_j\bigr)$, and the same expansion in the second and third coordinates gives $-\bigl(F\times\operatorname{curl}F\bigr)_i=\sum_{j=1}^{3}\bigl(F_j\partial_jF_i-F_j\partial_iF_j\bigr)$ for every $i$. Substituting this into step 2.1 gives $\operatorname{div}Q=F\operatorname{div}F-F\times\operatorname{curl}F$, which is the first identity.

At each time the field $(x\times\Pi)_{i\ell}=\epsilon_{ijk}x_j\Pi_{k\ell}$ is spatially $C^1$, and differentiating the product in $x_\ell$ and summing over $\ell$ gives $(\operatorname{div}(x\times\Pi))_i=\sum_{\ell=1}^{3}\partial_\ell(\epsilon_{ijk}x_j\Pi_{k\ell})=\epsilon_{ijk}\sum_{\ell=1}^{3}\bigl(\delta_{j\ell}\Pi_{k\ell}+x_j\partial_\ell\Pi_{k\ell}\bigr)=\epsilon_{ijk}\Pi_{kj}+\epsilon_{ijk}x_j\sum_{\ell=1}^{3}\partial_\ell\Pi_{k\ell}=\epsilon_{ijk}x_j(\operatorname{div}\Pi)_k$, where the term $\epsilon_{ijk}\Pi_{kj}$ vanishes by step 2.2 applied to the symmetric field $\Pi$; here $\delta_{j\ell}$ is the Kronecker symbol and the product rule [F4] was used in each summand.

Throughout, assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]); the surface integral of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]] and the domains of [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]] are developed under that convention.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open. Let $S\subset\Omega$ be a compact embedded $C^2$ hypersurface ([[def-codimension-and-hypersurface]], [[def-embedded-submanifold-and-slice-chart]]): every $p\in S$ has an open neighbourhood $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ and a $C^2$ diffeomorphism $\varphi:U\to\varphi(U)$ onto an open subset of $\mathbb R^3$ with $\varphi(S\cap U)=\varphi(U)\cap(\mathbb R^2\times\{0\})$, in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. Such an $S$ is a compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface, so the surface integral and the surface measure $S(A)=\int_S\mathbf 1_A\,dS$ of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]] and [[lem-surface-integral-is-independent-of-c-one-boundary-charts]] apply; that measure is finite. The slice-chart definition has no manifold boundary; $S$ has no edge. If $S$ is empty, all surface functionals below are zero and the estimates are read separately without taking a supremum over the empty set.

A **two-sided presentation** of $S$ consists of a continuous unit normal field $n:S\to\mathbb R^3$ together with sides: $n(x)$ is orthogonal to $S$ at $x$ in the sense that $\langle n(x),\gamma'(0)\rangle=0$ for every $C^1$ path $\gamma:(-1,1)\to S$ with $\gamma(0)=x$ and $\lVert n(x)\rVert_2=1$; and $\Omega_-,\Omega_+\subseteq\Omega$ are open sets with

$$\Omega\setminus S=\Omega_-\cup\Omega_+,\qquad \Omega_-\cap\Omega_+=\varnothing,$$

such that for every $x\in S$ there is $\varepsilon=\varepsilon(x)>0$ with $x+sn(x)\in\Omega_+$ for all $0<s<\varepsilon$ and $x+sn(x)\in\Omega_-$ for all $-\varepsilon<s<0$. The normal $n$ points from the side $\Omega_-$ to the side $\Omega_+$; the orientation convention for normals is that of [[def-oriented-unit-normal-and-flux-of-a-surface-patch]].

**The surface distribution $\delta_S$.** For $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]) define

$$\delta_S(\psi):=\int_S\psi\,dS,$$

where the right-hand side is the surface integral of the restriction of $\psi$ to $S$, taken in the sense of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]; complex-valued $\psi$ are integrated componentwise in real and imaginary parts. For a continuous **density** $a:S\to\mathbb R$ define

$$a\delta_S(\psi):=\int_S a\,\psi\,dS .$$

Both are complex-linear functionals on $\mathcal D(\Omega)$, and both are distributions: $\delta_S,a\delta_S\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ ([[def-distribution]]).

**Jumps across $S$.** Let $F:\Omega\setminus S\to\mathbb R^3$ be a field that is of class $C^1$ on $\Omega_-$ and on $\Omega_+$ separately and has one-sided continuous traces: there are continuous maps $F_+,F_-:S\to\mathbb R^3$ with

$$F_+(x)=\lim_{\substack{y\to x\\ y\in\Omega_+}}F(y),\qquad F_-(x)=\lim_{\substack{y\to x\\ y\in\Omega_-}}F(y)$$

for every $x\in S$, the limits taken in $\mathbb R^3$. The **jump of $F$ across $S$** is the continuous map

$$[F]:=F_+-F_-:S\to\mathbb R^3 .$$

No continuity of $F$ across $S$ is assumed or implied; $F$ need not even be defined on $S$, and the two traces may differ.

### Well-definedness and finite order

*The surface functionals are distributions.* Fix a compact $K\subseteq\Omega$ and $\psi\in\mathcal D_K=\{\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega):\operatorname{supp}\psi\subseteq K\}$ with the seminorm $p_0(\psi)=\sup_K|\psi|$ of [[def-fixed-support-test-function-frechet-space]]. Since $\psi$ vanishes outside $K$ and is continuous, $\sup_S|\psi|\le p_0(\psi)$; and $\int_S|a\psi|\,dS\le\lVert a\rVert_{\infty,S}\sup_S|\psi|\,S(S)$ with $\lVert a\rVert_{\infty,S}<\infty$ by compactness of $S$ and continuity of $a$. Hence

$$|\delta_S(\psi)|\le S(S)\,p_0(\psi),\qquad |a\delta_S(\psi)|\le \lVert a\rVert_{\infty,S}\,S(S)\,p_0(\psi),$$

a finite-order estimate of order $0$ with constants independent of $K$; by the local finite-order characterization ([[thm-local-finite-order-characterization-of-distributions]]) both functionals are distributions. This is the sense in which boundedness on the compact interface and finiteness of the surface measure give continuity of finite order. Linearity is immediate from linearity of the integral; the pairing is complex bilinear with no conjugation, as in [[def-distribution]].

*The field has locally integrable components.* The hypersurface $S$ is a Lebesgue-null set of $\mathbb R^3$: by the slice-chart property it is covered by finitely many compact pieces each of which is, in suitable $C^2$ coordinates, a graph over a compact subset of a coordinate plane, hence has content zero ([[thm-graph-of-continuous-function-on-a-compact-set-has-content-zero]]), and each piece has content zero in the ambient coordinates because it is the image under the $C^1$ chart inverse of a compact content-zero set ([[lem-c-one-images-of-content-zero-compact-sets-have-content-zero]]); a finite union of compact content-zero sets is compact and null ([[lem-null-sets-in-rn-closed-under-subsets-and-countable-unions]]), hence has content zero ([[lem-compact-null-iff-content-zero-in-rn]]), so $S$ has content zero in the sense of [[def-null-and-content-zero-in-rn]]. Now $F$ is continuous on $\Omega\setminus S=\Omega_-\cup\Omega_+$. For each $x\in S$, the two one-sided limits are finite; hence there is a neighbourhood $U_x$ of $x$ on which $|F|$ is bounded on each side (use the defining limit with tolerance $1$ for each of $F_+(x)$ and $F_-(x)$). Away from $S$, continuity also gives a neighbourhood with a finite bound at every point. For a compact $K\subseteq\Omega$, these neighbourhoods cover $K$; take a finite subcover and the maximum of its finitely many bounds. This gives a finite $M_K$ such that $|F|\le M_K$ on $K\setminus S$. Extend $F$ by zero on the null closed set $S$; the extension is measurable because the two side restrictions are continuous, and

$$\int_K\lVert F\rVert_2\le M_K\lambda_3(K)<\infty,$$

the contributions from $K\cap S$ being null. Thus the components of $F$ are locally integrable on $\Omega$ in the sense of [[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], and define a regular distribution; the trace condition is exactly what makes the boundary values $F_\pm$ well-defined continuous functions on $S$, so the jump $[F]$ is continuous and bounded on $S$.

### Conventions and exclusions

The sign convention is fixed by the normal: $n$ points from $\Omega_-$ to $\Omega_+$, so $[F]=F_+-F_-$ is measured in the direction of $n$. This convention is used by the interface-derivative lemma on this page, where $\operatorname{div}F$ and $\operatorname{curl}F$ acquire the surface terms $n\cdot[F]\,\delta_S$ and $n\times[F]\,\delta_S$; reversing $n$ reverses the signs of both sides consistently. The definition assumes a fixed stationary interface $S$: no time dependence of $S$ is part of the data, and the stationary jump formulas are not asserted for moving interfaces. The density $a$ is continuous, so $a\delta_S$ is defined by the displayed integral; no product of two arbitrary distributions, and no product of $\delta_S$ with a merely locally integrable field, is defined here. The definition is stated under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ because the surface measure it invokes is; the positivity of the surface measure of nonempty open pieces of $S$, and the finite-order estimates above, are its only uses here.

For a distribution $u\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ in the convention of [[def-distribution]] and a multi-index $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$, its **distributional derivative** is
$$\langle\partial^\alpha u,\varphi\rangle=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\langle u,\partial^\alpha\varphi\rangle\qquad(\varphi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)).$$
The test derivative is a continuous linear endomorphism by [[thm-test-function-operations-are-continuous]]. Its composition with $u$, multiplied by the indicated sign, is therefore a continuous complex-linear functional, so this definition produces a distribution. The pairing is bilinear, with no complex conjugation. For $\alpha=0$ the operation is the identity; for one coordinate derivative its sign is minus. Every derivative of the zero distribution is zero, including on the empty domain. No choice axiom enters this construction. Compatibility with classical derivatives requires an integration-by-parts argument where it is used; it is not part of the definition.

For open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, write $f\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ when $f:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is Lebesgue measurable and $\int_K|f|<\infty$ for every compact $K\subseteq\Omega$. This extends [[def-locally-integrable-function-on-r-n]]: equivalently, require integrability on every ball whose closure is a compact subset of $\Omega$. Such balls finitely cover each compact $K$, and conversely their closures are compact; on all of $\mathbb R^n$, any ball lies in a larger compact closed ball.

For a test $\varphi$ as in [[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]], define the **regular functional**

$$\langle u_f,\varphi\rangle=\int_\Omega f(x)\varphi(x)\,dx.$$

This is well-defined since $|\int f\varphi|\le\sup_K|\varphi|\int_K|f|$ for $K=\operatorname{supp}\varphi$. It is complex-linear in $f$ and in $\varphi$ and depends only on the almost-everywhere class of $f$. For an empty support the integral is zero. The subsequent embedding theorem establishes continuity, so that this is a distribution, and injectivity modulo almost-everywhere equality. That theorem states the Countable Choice cost of its injectivity proof; no choice is needed to define the displayed pairing.

For open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, a **distribution** is a continuous complex-linear map $u:\mathcal D(\Omega)\to\mathbb C$, with the test-function topology of [[def-test-function-topology]]. Their vector space is denoted $\mathcal D'(\Omega)$. Write $\langle u,\varphi\rangle=u(\varphi)$; the pairing is linear in both arguments, with no conjugation.

Continuity means continuity for that topology: for each $\varepsilon>0$ the set $\{|u(\varphi)|<\varepsilon\}$ contains a zero-neighborhood. By linearity this suffices at every point. Sums and scalar multiples remain continuous and linear, so the indicated collection is a complex vector space. If $\Omega=\varnothing$, its test space is zero and its distribution space is zero as well. The finite-order estimate and the sequential criterion are established separately; neither substitutes for continuity in this definition.

Under the $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ convention of [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]], a finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation of a nonempty bounded open $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, consists of compact faces $S_1,\ldots,S_q$ covering its boundary, each a compact Borel subset of a regular $C^1$ hypersurface patch, and a compact edge set $E\subset\partial\Omega$. Require $S_j\cap E$ to have surface measure zero in each face, using [[lem-surface-integral-is-independent-of-c-one-boundary-charts]]. E contains the boundaries of the faces relative to their patches and every overlap $S_i\cap S_j$, i different from j. At every point outside E the domain boundary is locally a single $C^1$ graph with Omega on one side. Each face carries this actual outward unit normal off E. Values assigned to the normal on E do not affect its integral.

For a specified finite gluing also list the open pieces with disjoint interiors, the shared faces, and their opposite outward normals. Require the pieces to cover the final domain up to their boundary faces, and the exposed faces to give its specified presentation. Internal faces are counted twice before cancellation, once from each side. The phrase piecewise smooth by itself supplies none of this data.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. If Omega has the specified finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation and $F\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^n)$, then $\int_\Omega\operatorname{div}F=\sum_j\int_{S_j}F\cdot\nu_j\,dS$, with faces counted once off E. All integrals are finite. In a specified finite gluing, the two fluxes on every shared face cancel.

Assume the $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ convention of [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]. Let S be a compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface in $\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$. Choose finitely many regular injective $C^1$ parametrizations $X_j:V_j\to S\cap O_j$ with $C^1$ coordinate transitions, and an ambient partition $\chi_j$ from [[lem-finite-ambient-partitions-for-euclidean-boundary-integration]], with supports compactly contained in the corresponding chart neighborhoods. Put $J_{X_j}=\sqrt{\det(DX_j^TDX_j)}$, using [[def-gram-matrix-and-gram-determinant]].

For a nonnegative Borel f on S define $\int_S f\,dS=\sum_j\int_{V_j}(\chi_j f)(X_j(y))J_{X_j}(y)\,dy$, where the integrals on the right are those of [[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]] and $0\cdot\infty=0$. Set $S(A)=\int_S\mathbf1_A\,dS$ for Borel A. For signed f with $\int_S|f|\,dS<\infty$ use the difference of the positive and negative integrals. The same chart formula restricts to a compact Borel face contained in a regular patch. The empty surface has zero integral. Independence and finiteness are established by the following chart-independence lemma.

In ZF, for compact $K\subseteq\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $\Omega$ open, there is $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ with $0\le\chi\le1$ and $\chi=1$ on a neighborhood of $K$. Every open cover of $\Omega$ admits an at most countable locally finite smooth partition of unity with compact supports, each support contained in some cover member. Subordination here asserts existence of such a member for each support; it does not select cover labels.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $F=(F_0,\ldots,F_{n-1}):U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$ in the componentwise Euclidean sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. Then the **divergence** of $F$ is $\operatorname{div}F:=\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i$, the function $U\to\mathbb R$ whose value at $p$ is $\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i(p)$. The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], and the sum is the finite sum used throughout [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Since each $\partial_iF_i$ is continuous on $U$, so is $\operatorname{div}F$.

Now let $n=3$ and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^1$ on an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$. Following [[def-cross-product-in-r3]], write the three coordinates of a point and of a vector as $x,y,z$ rather than $0,1,2$, so that $F=(F_x,F_y,F_z)$ means $F=(F_0,F_1,F_2)$ and $\partial_x,\partial_y,\partial_z$ are $\partial_0,\partial_1,\partial_2$. With that naming, the **curl** of $F$ is $\operatorname{curl}F:=(\partial_yF_z-\partial_zF_y,\ \partial_zF_x-\partial_xF_z,\ \partial_xF_y-\partial_yF_x)$, a map $U\to\mathbb R^3$ each of whose coordinates is continuous on $U$. In this naming the divergence reads $\operatorname{div}F=\partial_xF_x+\partial_yF_y+\partial_zF_z$.

Both operators are defined pointwise from the first partial derivatives of the components, so no differentiability of $F$ beyond $C^1$ is used and no orientation or metric structure enters beyond the standard coordinates of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]. For a $C^1$ scalar function $f$ on $U$, the gradient $\nabla f=(\partial_0f,\ldots,\partial_{n-1}f)$ is that of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]; in the three-coordinate naming, $\nabla f=(\partial_xf,\partial_yf,\partial_zf)$.

For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$.

This is the right-handed **cross product**. The displayed coordinates are those of the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), and inner products and norms are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A bijection $f:U\to V$ is a **$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $C^k$. For $k\ge1$, a **local $C^k$ diffeomorphism at $a\in U$** is a restriction $f|_P:P\to Q$ between open neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$ that is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism. At $k=1$ this agrees with [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: continuous first partial derivatives give the required total derivative by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], while continuity of the total derivative gives continuity of its matrix entries and hence of the first partial derivatives.

derivations.claim: By [F1] the components of $F$ and of its one-sided first derivatives are locally integrable on $\Omega$, the piecewise fields $\{\partial_iF_j\}$ are locally integrable, and $[F_j]$ is continuous on $S$; hence all the distributions displayed in the Statement are defined, and $n_i[F_j]\delta_S$ is the surface distribution of the continuous density $n_i[F_j]$ of [F1].

Reduction to finite chart boxes. At a point of $S$ use the $C^2$ slice diffeomorphism $\phi$ from [F1], with $\phi(S)=\{s=0\}$ locally. Choose a closed rectangular product box inside its open image, centred at the image point, and write $B$ for its open inverse image. Shrink the box so its closure is compactly contained in the chart and in $\Omega$. The two sets $B_\pm=B\cap\Omega_\pm$ are inverse images of the two open half-boxes: the local side designation is determined by the normal convention and continuity, and the half-boxes are connected. Each has a specified finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation, with the interface rectangle at $s=0$ and the finitely many outer rectangular faces transported by the $C^2$ chart inverse. Faces are regular parametrized compact patches. Their seams are transported line segments and vertices, hence null in ambient volume: the chart inverse has bounded first derivatives on the compact box, so a subdivision of each segment into $O(\delta^{-1})$ pieces has images covered by balls of radius $C\delta$, whose total three-dimensional content is $O(\delta^2)\to0$. For the required surface-null condition, parametrize each face by its two free box coordinates. Its seam preimage is a finite union of line segments, covered by $O(\delta^{-1})$ parameter squares of area $O(\delta^2)$; thus it has two-dimensional Lebesgue measure zero. The chart surface density is bounded on the compact face, so its surface integral on those seams is zero. This verifies the finite-face and seam obligations in [F3], without asserting any property of a spherical chart cut. Compactness of the test support and [F4] now give finitely many such $B_1,\dots,B_N$ covering $\operatorname{supp}\psi\cap S$, with compactly supported smooth cutoffs $\chi_k$ inside $B_k$ summing to one near that intersection. Write $\psi=\sum_k\chi_k\psi+(1-\sum_k\chi_k)\psi$; the last test vanishes near $S$, where the identity is the ordinary classical integration-by-parts identity. Thus it suffices to prove the displayed component identity for a test supported in one $B_k$.

Local computation: let $\varphi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$ have support in a chart box $B=B_k$ as in step 1.2. By [F2], $\langle\partial_iF_j,\varphi\rangle=-\int_{\Omega}F_j\partial_i\varphi=-\int_{\Omega_+}F_j\partial_i\varphi-\int_{\Omega_-}F_j\partial_i\varphi$. On each side apply the divergence theorem [F3] to $G^\pm:=F_j\varphi\,e_i$. Its values and first spatial derivatives extend continuously to the closed half-box by the one-sided trace hypothesis and the product rule, so it belongs to $C^1(\overline{B_\pm})$ in the stated up-to-boundary convention, which requires no ambient extension. It vanishes near every outer box face because $\operatorname{supp}\varphi\subseteq B$. For complex $\varphi$, apply the real divergence theorem separately to its real and imaginary parts; the outward normal of $\Omega_+$ on the interface face is $-n$ and that of $\Omega_-$ is $+n$, so $\int_{\Omega_+}\partial_i(F_j\varphi)=-\int_{S\cap B}(F_j)_+\varphi\,n_i\,dS$ and $\int_{\Omega_-}\partial_i(F_j\varphi)=\int_{S\cap B}(F_j)_-\varphi\,n_i\,dS$. A nonempty open set $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ is **star-shaped with respect to** $a\in U$ when

$$a+t(x-a)\in U\qquad\text{for every }x\in U\text{ and }0\le t\le1.$$

The point $a$ is a **star centre**. Every convex open set of [[def-convex-subset-of-euclidean-space]] is star-shaped with respect to each of its points. The nonemptiness and the chosen centre are part of the definition.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open and let $B:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be continuous. Given a map $A:U\to\mathbb R^3$, we say $A$ is a **vector potential** for $B$ when $A$ is $C^1$ on $U$ and $\operatorname{curl}A=B$ at every point of $U$, with the curl of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and the class $C^1$ of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. A field admitting a vector potential is said to **have a vector potential** on $U$.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open and star-shaped with star centre $a$, and let $B:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^1$ with $\operatorname{div}B=0$ on $U$. Then $B$ has a vector potential on $U$ in the sense of [[def-vector-potential-of-a-c1-vector-field]]: the map

$$A(x):=\int_0^1t\,B\bigl(a+t(x-a)\bigr)\times(x-a)\,dt\qquad(x\in U),$$

understood coordinatewise, is $C^1$ on $U$ and satisfies $\operatorname{curl}A=B$.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and star-shaped with respect to $a\in U$. Every closed $C^1$ field $F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ is exact. A $C^2$ potential is

$$\phi(x):=\int_0^1\left\langle F(a+t(x-a)),x-a\right\rangle\,dt.$$

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $F=(F_0,\ldots,F_{n-1}):U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$. Coordinates and partial derivatives are indexed from $0$ throughout, as in [[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] and [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]. It is **exact** when $F=\nabla\phi$ for some $C^2$ scalar function $\phi:U\to\mathbb R$, using the gradient of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]. It is **closed** when

$$\partial_jF_i=\partial_iF_j\qquad(i,j<n),$$

where the partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. The $C^2$ requirement in exactness makes all mixed second partials of the potential available and continuous.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A bijection $f:U\to V$ is a **$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $C^k$. For $k\ge1$, a **local $C^k$ diffeomorphism at $a\in U$** is a restriction $f|_P:P\to Q$ between open neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$ that is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism. At $k=1$ this agrees with [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: continuous first partial derivatives give the required total derivative by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], while continuity of the total derivative gives continuity of its matrix entries and hence of the first partial derivatives.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $a<b$ and $c<d$. Suppose $g,h:[a,b]\times[c,d]\to\mathbb R$ are continuous and, for every fixed $t\in[c,d]$, the function $x\mapsto g(x,t)$ is differentiable on $(a,b)$ with derivative $h(x,t)$. Define

$$G(x):=\int_c^d g(x,t)\,dt.$$

Then $G$ is differentiable on $[a,b]$ as a function on that interval and

$$G'(x)=\int_c^d h(x,t)\,dt\qquad(x\in[a,b]).$$

At $a$ and $b$ the derivative is relative and one-sided. The derivative hypothesis is imposed only for interior parameter values; continuity of $h$ supplies its endpoint values.

Let $(X,d_X)$ be a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]]), let
$(Y,d_Y)$ be any metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to Y$ be
continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]). Then $f$ is uniformly continuous
([[def-metric-uniform-continuity]]).

No choice principle is used: the cover built below is cut out by a property, and
the Lebesgue number lemma it is fed to is itself choice free
([[thm-lebesgue-number-lemma]]).

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $u,v\in\mathbb{R}$, and let $f$ and $g$ be integrable between $u$ and $v$.
If $\eta\ge0$ and

$$|f(x)-g(x)|\le\eta$$

throughout the closed interval with endpoints $u$ and $v$, then

$$\left|\int_u^v f-\int_u^v g\right|\le \eta\,|v-u|.$$

Let $a<b$. Suppose $G:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$. If $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is Riemann integrable and

$$f(x)=G'(x)\qquad(a<x<b),$$

then

$$\int_a^b f=G(b)-G(a).$$

No derivative of $G$ at either endpoint is assumed, and the two endpoint values assigned to the integrable extension $f$ do not enter the conclusion.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ be a nonempty finite elementary Green region in the sense of [[def-type-i-type-ii-and-elementary-green-regions]], written as $D=D_1\cup\cdots\cup D_N$ with its supplied decomposition into elementary Green regions of pairwise disjoint interiors and with the shared-arc structure of that definition, and let $\partial D$ be its positive boundary chain ([[def-positive-orientation-for-elementary-region-boundaries]]). We require in addition that $D$ be Jordan measurable; this is explained below and holds for every finite elementary Green region. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval and let

$$r:D\times I\to\mathbb R^3$$

be a map that extends to a $C^2$ map ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]) on an open neighbourhood of $D\times I\subseteq\mathbb R^3$. Write $p=(u,v)$ for the parameter point, write $r_u(p,t),r_v(p,t),r_t(p,t)\in\mathbb R^3$ for the partial derivatives of that $C^2$ extension at $(p,t)$, and require

$$r_u(p,t)\times r_v(p,t)\ne0\qquad\text{for every }(p,t)\in D^\circ\times I^\circ,$$

the cross product being that of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]. For every $t\in I^\circ$ this gives rank two on $D^\circ$. It does not imply the connectedness or interior injectivity required by [[def-admissible-regular-parametrized-surface-patch]]; neither is a standing hypothesis here. At endpoint or singleton times the rank condition is not imposed.

The **swept set** of the family is

$$S:=\bigcup_{t\in I}r(D\times\{t\})\subseteq\mathbb R^3,\qquad \Sigma:=\{(r(p,t),t):p\in D,\ t\in I\}\subseteq\mathbb R^4 .$$

A **velocity field for $r$** is a pair $(W,v)$ consisting of an open set $W\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ with $\Sigma\subseteq W$ and a map $v:W\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^1$ such that

$$v\bigl(r(p,t),t\bigr)=r_t(p,t)\qquad\text{for every }(p,t)\in D\times I .$$

Such a pair is required to exist: the standing hypothesis of this definition is that a velocity field for $r$ is given, and $v$ denotes it. The equality above is what single-valuedness means here: whenever two parameter points at the same time map to the same spatial point, their time derivatives agree. Values at different times may differ.

Finally let $B:V\to\mathbb R^3$ be a $C^1$ field on an open set $V\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ containing $\Sigma$. The **flux of $B$ through the patch at time $t\in I$** is

$$\Phi(t):=\int_D\bigl\langle B\bigl(r(p,t),t\bigr),\,r_u(p,t)\times r_v(p,t)\bigr\rangle\,du\,dv,$$

the integral being the Riemann integral over the compact Jordan measurable set $D$ of the displayed continuous integrand, and the pairing being the Euclidean inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. This is a parametrized flux, counted with the supplied parametrization. When $(D,r(\cdot,t))$ satisfies the regular-patch definition, it agrees with [[def-oriented-unit-normal-and-flux-of-a-surface-patch]]. In general different parameter points may represent the same spatial point with different normals. At a rank-two slice the unit normal means $N(p,t)=(r_u\times r_v)/\lVert r_u\times r_v\rVert_2$ on $D^\circ$, not necessarily a function of the spatial image alone.

For an injectively parametrized material-sheet interpretation, require in addition that $r(\cdot,t):D\to\mathbb R^3$ be injective for every $t\in I$. Injectivity alone does not imply $r_u\times r_v\ne0$: a regular-slice interpretation also requires this condition on $D^\circ\times I$, including endpoint and singleton times. These additional requirements are not standing hypotheses and are not used by the flux formula above.

### Well-definedness and conventions

*Jordan measurability of $D$.* Each piece is compact and Jordan measurable by [[def-type-i-type-ii-and-elementary-green-regions]]. The topological boundary of their finite union is contained in the finite union of their content-zero boundaries: a point outside all those boundaries is either interior to one piece or exterior to every piece. Combining finite cube covers proves content zero without Countable Choice. Thus $D$ is compact and Jordan measurable by [[thm-jordan-boundary-criterion]]; the positive boundary chain $\partial D$ is separate supplied orientation data.

*Extension independence.* Each elementary piece is the closure of its interior by its strict graph inequalities, so $D=\overline{D^\circ}$. Two $C^2$ extensions agree on $D\times I$, and their spatial difference quotients agree at interior parameter points. Their continuous spatial partials therefore agree on all of $D\times I$: a nonzero difference at a boundary point would remain nonzero nearby and contradict the dense-interior equality. For nondegenerate $I$, the same argument on the dense set $D^\circ\times I^\circ$ makes $r_t$ extension-independent. For singleton $I=\{t_0\}$ it does not: the same zero restriction admits extensions $0$ and $(t-t_0)\chi(p)$ with different time derivatives. In that case the chosen extension is part of the velocity data; the flux still depends only on the spatial partials.

*Integrability.* For fixed $t\in I$, the map $p\mapsto B(r(p,t),t)$ is continuous on $D$ as a composition of continuous maps, the maps $p\mapsto r_u(p,t)$ and $p\mapsto r_v(p,t)$ are continuous on $D$, and the cross product and inner product are continuous bilinear operations; hence the integrand is continuous on the compact set $D$. A continuous real function on a compact Jordan measurable set is Riemann integrable over it ([[thm-continuous-functions-on-compact-jordan-sets-are-integrable]]), so $\Phi(t)$ is defined for every $t\in I$.

*Degenerate time domains.* If $I$ is empty then $D\times I$ is empty, the family is vacuous and no flux value is asserted. If $I=\{t_0\}$ is a singleton, the compatibility condition still reads $v(r(p,t_0),t_0)=r_t(p,t_0)$, but it can always be met: choosing the extension $\tilde r(p,t):=r(p,t_0)$, which is constant in the time variable, gives $r_t\equiv0$ and admits the compatible $C^1$ velocity field $v\equiv0$. A different extension may require a different velocity field or may fail compatibility; as explained above, $r_t(p,t_0)$ is not determined by $r$ alone in this case. The flux $\Phi(t_0)$ involves only $r_u\times r_v$, so it is the parametrized flux of the fixed map and does not depend on that choice. The condition $r_u\times r_v\ne0$ is imposed only on $D^\circ\times I^\circ$, so rank failures on the boundary of the parameter region (seams) are permitted exactly as in [[def-admissible-regular-parametrized-surface-patch]], and at an endpoint time of a nondegenerate $I$ the definition asserts no regularity of the slice.

*No physical assertion.* This is a definition of a mathematical object: a time-dependent parametrized family, a velocity field compatible with it, and the flux integral. It asserts nothing about electromagnetic fields, about which vector fields occur in nature, or about the derivative of $\Phi$; the transport identity for $\Phi'$ is proved separately.

**Set form.** Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, [[def-countable-choice]]), used to establish the Lebesgue measure space of [[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]. Let $K\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be compact, Lebesgue measurable and of finite Lebesgue measure $\lambda_n(K)<\infty$, let $a<b$, and let $f$ be a real-valued function, defined and continuous together with its partial derivative $\partial_tf$ on an open neighbourhood of $K\times[a,b]$ in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$. Then $t\mapsto\int_Kf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x)$ is differentiable at every $t\in(a,b)$ with

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_Kf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x)=\int_K\partial_tf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x),$$

and at $t=a$ and $t=b$ it has relative (one-sided) derivatives, taken within $[a,b]$, both equal to the same displayed integral. Equivalently, for every $t\in[a,b]$ and every sequence $h_k\to0$ with $h_k\ne0$ and $t+h_k\in[a,b]$,

$$\lim_{k\to\infty}\frac{1}{h_k}\Bigl(\int_Kf(x,t+h_k)\,d\lambda_n(x)-\int_Kf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x)\Bigr)=\int_K\partial_tf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x).$$

**Surface form.** Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, [[def-countable-choice]]) for the surface measure of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]. Let $S$ be a fixed compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface in $\mathbb R^m$, $m\ge2$, and let $f$ be real-valued, defined and continuous together with $\partial_tf$ on an open neighbourhood of $S\times[a,b]$. Then $t\mapsto\int_Sf(\sigma,t)\,dS(\sigma)$ is differentiable in the same relative sense with

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_Sf(\sigma,t)\,dS(\sigma)=\int_S\partial_tf(\sigma,t)\,dS(\sigma).$$

The statements are pointwise in $t$ and make no claim about moving parameter sets $K(t)$ or $S(t)$, about singularities crossing $K$ or $S$, about differentiability of $\partial_tf$, or about differentiation in the spatial variables; only the one-dimensional parameter $t$ is differentiated. Integrals are Lebesgue integrals, and the surface integrals are those of the cited surface measure; the case $K=\varnothing$ or $\lambda_n(K)=0$ is included and the two sides vanish.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $n\ge1$, let $Q=\prod_{j=1}^n[a_j,b_j]$ with $a_j<b_j$, and let $f:Q\to\mathbb R$ be bounded and Borel. If $f$ is Riemann integrable, then $f\in L^1(\lambda_n|_Q)$ and its Lebesgue and Riemann integrals agree.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].
If $f$ is $C^2$ on an open subset of $\mathbb R^m$, then $\partial_i\partial_j f=\partial_j\partial_i f$ for every pair of coordinate indices.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A bijection $f:U\to V$ is a **$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $C^k$. For $k\ge1$, a **local $C^k$ diffeomorphism at $a\in U$** is a restriction $f|_P:P\to Q$ between open neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$ that is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism. At $k=1$ this agrees with [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: continuous first partial derivatives give the required total derivative by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], while continuity of the total derivative gives continuity of its matrix entries and hence of the first partial derivatives.

For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$.

This is the right-handed **cross product**. The displayed coordinates are those of the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), and inner products and norms are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].
For all $u,v,w\in\mathbb R^3$, the cross product is bilinear and alternating, $\langle u\times v,w\rangle=\det[u\ v\ w]$, and $u\times v$ is orthogonal to both $u$ and $v$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Fix $n\ge1$ and a commutative ring $R$. A function $F:M_n(R)\to R$ is **column-multilinear** when, with all other columns fixed, it is additive and compatible with scalar multiplication in each selected column.

It is **alternating** when $F(A)=0$ whenever two columns of $A$ are equal. It is **antisymmetric** when interchanging two columns negates its value. It is **normalized** when $F(I_n)=1$. These conditions are stated over the ring itself and do not assume that $2$ is invertible.

Let $n\ge1$, let $R$ be a commutative ring, and let $F:M_n(R)\to R$ be alternating and column-multilinear. Then for $A=(a_{ri})$,
$$F(A)=F(I_n)\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\prod_{i<n}a_{\sigma(i),i}.$$

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $F=(F_0,\ldots,F_{n-1}):U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$ in the componentwise Euclidean sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. Then the **divergence** of $F$ is $\operatorname{div}F:=\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i$, the function $U\to\mathbb R$ whose value at $p$ is $\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i(p)$. The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], and the sum is the finite sum used throughout [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Since each $\partial_iF_i$ is continuous on $U$, so is $\operatorname{div}F$.

Now let $n=3$ and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^1$ on an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$. Following [[def-cross-product-in-r3]], write the three coordinates of a point and of a vector as $x,y,z$ rather than $0,1,2$, so that $F=(F_x,F_y,F_z)$ means $F=(F_0,F_1,F_2)$ and $\partial_x,\partial_y,\partial_z$ are $\partial_0,\partial_1,\partial_2$. With that naming, the **curl** of $F$ is $\operatorname{curl}F:=(\partial_yF_z-\partial_zF_y,\ \partial_zF_x-\partial_xF_z,\ \partial_xF_y-\partial_yF_x)$, a map $U\to\mathbb R^3$ each of whose coordinates is continuous on $U$. In this naming the divergence reads $\operatorname{div}F=\partial_xF_x+\partial_yF_y+\partial_zF_z$.

Both operators are defined pointwise from the first partial derivatives of the components, so no differentiability of $F$ beyond $C^1$ is used and no orientation or metric structure enters beyond the standard coordinates of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]. For a $C^1$ scalar function $f$ on $U$, the gradient $\nabla f=(\partial_0f,\ldots,\partial_{n-1}f)$ is that of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]; in the three-coordinate naming, $\nabla f=(\partial_xf,\partial_yf,\partial_zf)$.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open and let $F,G:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^1$. Then $F\times G$ is $C^1$ on $U$ and

$$\operatorname{div}(F\times G)=\langle\operatorname{curl}F,G\rangle-\langle F,\operatorname{curl}G\rangle,$$

$$\operatorname{curl}(F\times G)=(\operatorname{div}G)F-(\operatorname{div}F)G+DF\,G-DG\,F.$$

Here $DF\,G$ denotes the map $U\to\mathbb R^3$ whose $i$th coordinate at $p$ is $\sum_{j<3}\partial_jF_i(p)\,G_j(p)$, that is, the Jacobian matrix of $F$ at $p$ applied to the vector $G(p)$, and $DG\,F$ is defined the same way with the roles of $F$ and $G$ exchanged. The operators are those of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]], the cross product is that of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]], the inner product that of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and the Jacobian matrix that of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]].

Let $O\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ be open, let $\varphi:O\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^2$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open with $\varphi[O]\subseteq U$ and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^1$. Put $P^{*}=\langle F\circ\varphi,\varphi_u\rangle$ and $Q^{*}=\langle F\circ\varphi,\varphi_v\rangle$ on $O$. Then $P^{*}$ and $Q^{*}$ are $C^1$ on $O$ and, at every point of $O$, the difference of the two pulled-back partial derivatives equals the curl flux integrand:

$$\partial_uQ^{*}-\partial_vP^{*}=\bigl\langle(\operatorname{curl}F)\circ\varphi,\ \varphi_u\times\varphi_v\bigr\rangle.$$

No regularity of the patch is used: the identity holds also at parameter points where $\varphi_u\times\varphi_v=0$.

Let $D=D_1\cup\cdots\cup D_N$ be a finite elementary Green region with its supplied decomposition, and orient $\partial D$ positively. If $P,Q$ are $C^1$ on an open neighbourhood of $D$, then

$$\int_{\partial D}P\,dx+Q\,dy=\iint_D\left(\partial_xQ-\partial_yP\right)dA.$$

Let $O\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ be open, let $\varphi:O\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^1$, let $\sigma=(\sigma_1,\sigma_2):[a,b]\to O$ be a piecewise-$C^1$ path, and let $F$ be a continuous vector field on a set containing $\varphi(\sigma([a,b]))$. Put $P^{*}=\langle F\circ\varphi,\varphi_u\rangle$ and $Q^{*}=\langle F\circ\varphi,\varphi_v\rangle$ where these are defined. Then $\varphi\circ\sigma$ is a piecewise-$C^1$ path in $\mathbb R^3$ and the vector line integral of the field along the image arc equals the parameter line integral of the pulled-back pair:

$$\int_{\varphi\circ\sigma}F\cdot d\mathbf r=\int_{\sigma}(P^{*},Q^{*})\cdot d\mathbf r.$$

Let $(D,\varphi)$ be a regular surface patch and let $q$ be a continuous real-valued function on $\varphi[D]$. For a continuous scalar field $q$ on the patch image, $\int_Sq\,dS:=\int_D(q\circ\varphi)J_\varphi$, and $\operatorname{Area}(S):=\int_DJ_\varphi$.

Here $S$ denotes the patch with its chosen parametrization. Both integrands are bounded and Riemann integrable on the compact Jordan region $D$ by continuity ([[thm-continuous-functions-on-compact-jordan-sets-are-integrable]]). Boundary values are included in the parameter integral but may be changed on the content-zero boundary without changing its value.

For every parameter point, $J_\varphi=\|\varphi_u\times\varphi_v\|_2$.

The common value is positive in the interior of a regular patch; it may vanish on the parameter boundary under the admitted seam and endpoint convention.

For a regular patch $(D,\varphi)$, the parametrization induces on its interior the unit normal
$$N_\varphi=\frac{\varphi_u\times\varphi_v}{\|\varphi_u\times\varphi_v\|_2}.$$
The denominator is positive there by regularity and [[thm-surface-area-density-is-cross-product-norm]], and the vector is orthogonal to the tangent plane ([[def-tangent-plane-of-a-regular-surface-patch]]). Choosing $N_\varphi$ rather than $-N_\varphi$ is an **orientation**.

For a continuous vector field $F$, the flux in the orientation induced by $\varphi$ is $\int_D(F\circ\varphi)\cdot(\varphi_u\times\varphi_v)$. This is the scalar Riemann integral of a continuous function on $D$ ([[def-surface-area-and-scalar-surface-integral-of-a-patch]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]); replacing the orientation by its negative negates the integrand.

derivations.claim: Preliminaries. The integrand $h(p,t):=\langle B(r(p,t),t),w(p,t)\rangle$ is defined for $(p,t)$ in a neighbourhood of $D\times I$ and is continuous there together with $\partial_th$: $r$ and its first derivatives are continuous, $B$ is $C^1$ on an open spacetime neighbourhood of the swept graph, and sums, products and compositions of continuous maps are continuous. Moreover $\tilde v(p,t)=r_t(p,t)=v(r(p,t),t)$ is $C^1$ in $(p,t)$, so $D_xv$ denotes the spatial Jacobian of the velocity field, evaluated at $r(p,t)$, and $\operatorname{div}v$ its spatial divergence; at an interior time or a rank-two endpoint slice the vector $w=r_u\times r_v$ does not vanish on $D^\circ$, so the unit normal $N=w/\lVert w\rVert_2$ is defined there.

Algebraic identity for the area vector. For every $3\times3$ real matrix $A$ and all $B_0,u_1,u_2\in\mathbb R^3$, $\langle B_0,(Au_1)\times u_2\rangle+\langle B_0,u_1\times(Au_2)\rangle=\operatorname{tr}(A)\langle B_0,u_1\times u_2\rangle-\langle AB_0,u_1\times u_2\rangle$. To prove it, let $M=[m_1\ m_2\ m_3]$ range over $3\times3$ matrices and put $E(M):=\langle m_1,(Am_2)\times m_3\rangle+\langle m_1,m_2\times(Am_3)\rangle-\operatorname{tr}(A)\langle m_1,m_2\times m_3\rangle+\langle Am_1,m_2\times m_3\rangle$. Each of the four terms is linear in each column separately: the triple product is trilinear by [F4] and multiplication by the fixed matrix $A$ is linear, so $E$ is column-multilinear. Writing the four terms as the determinants $T_1=\det[m_1,Am_2,m_3]$, $T_2=\det[m_1,m_2,Am_3]$, $T_3=-\operatorname{tr}(A)\det[m_1,m_2,m_3]$ and $T_4=\det[Am_1,m_2,m_3]$ by [F4], each interchange of two of the columns $m_1,m_2,m_3$ carries every $T_i$ to $\pm$ one of the four terms in such a way that the total reverses sign: for example exchanging the first two columns sends $T_1$ to $-T_4$, $T_4$ to $-T_1$, and $T_2,T_3$ to their own negatives, so $E\mapsto-E$; the other two interchanges are verified by the same determinant expansion. Hence $E$ is alternating as well. Therefore [F5] gives $E(M)=E(I_3)\det(M)$ for every $M$, and $E(I_3)=A_{22}+A_{33}-\operatorname{tr}(A)+A_{11}=0$, because $\langle e_1,Ae_2\times e_3\rangle=A_{22}$, $\langle e_1,e_2\times Ae_3\rangle=A_{33}$ and $\langle Ae_1,e_2\times e_3\rangle=A_{11}$ computed from the coordinate formula of [F4]. Hence $E\equiv0$, which is the displayed identity at $(B_0,u_1,u_2)=(m_1,m_2,m_3)$.

Differentiation of the flux. Since $h$ and $\partial_th$ are continuous on a neighbourhood of $D\times I$, use [F2] on any local compact time segment with $K=D$; its Riemann/Lebesgue bridge identifies both parameter integrals and gives that $\Phi$ is differentiable on $I$, with relative one-sided derivatives at included endpoints, and $\Phi'(t)=\int_D\partial_th(p,t)\,dp$.

The derivative of the integrand. Since $r_t=\tilde v$ and $\tilde v(p,t)=v(r(p,t),t)$, the chain rule [F3] gives $\partial_tr_u=\partial_u r_t=(D_xv)r_u$ and $\partial_tr_v=(D_xv)r_v$, so, using equality of mixed partials for the $C^2$ map $r$, $\partial_tw=((D_xv)r_u)\times r_v+r_u\times((D_xv)r_v)$; and $\partial_t\bigl[B(r(p,t),t)\bigr]=\partial_tB(r(p,t),t)+(D_xB)r_t$ by the chain rule. Hence, multiplying out and evaluating the spatial derivatives at $r(p,t)$, $\partial_th=\langle\partial_tB+(D_xB)\tilde v,w\rangle+\langle B,\partial_tw\rangle=\langle\partial_tB+(D_xB)v+(\operatorname{div}v)B-(D_xv)B,\ w\rangle$, the last equality by step 1.2 with $A:=D_xv$, $B_0:=B$, $(u_1,u_2):=(r_u,r_v)$.

Conversion by the cross-product identity. By [F6] with $F:=v$ and $G:=B$, $\operatorname{curl}(v\times B)=(\operatorname{div}B)v-(\operatorname{div}v)B+(Dv)B-(DB)v$, where $(Dv)B=(D_xv)B$ and $(DB)v=(D_xB)v$; substituting into step 2.2 gives $\partial_th=\langle\partial_tB+v\,\operatorname{div}B-\operatorname{curl}(v\times B),\ w\rangle$.

Parametric Stokes and conclusion. Fix a time $t$ of the nondegenerate $I$. The spatial slices of $v,B$ are $C^1$ on the open slice of $W\cap V$ containing $r(D,t)$; hence $G=(v\times B)(\cdot,t)$ is $C^1$ there. Restrict the $C^2$ extension of $\varphi=r(\cdot,t)$ to an open neighbourhood $O\supseteq D$ mapping into that slice. The first supplier in [F7] makes $P^*,Q^*$ $C^1$ on $O$ with the displayed curl integrand. Green then gives its integral over $D$ as the positive boundary integral, and the pullback supplier identifies each arc integral with $\int_{\varphi\circ\sigma_\ell}G\cdot d\mathbf r$. Thus $\int_D\langle\operatorname{curl}(v\times B)(r,t),w\rangle\,dp=\oint_{\partial S(t)}(v\times B)\cdot d\mathbf r$ without requiring a published regular patch. Substituting into steps 2.1 and 3.1 gives the always-defined parameter identity $\Phi'(t)=\int_D\langle\partial_tB(r,t)+v(r,t)\operatorname{div}B(r,t),w\rangle\,dp-\oint_{\partial S(t)}(v\times B)\cdot d\mathbf r$. At a rank-two slice its first two integrals are exactly the surface shorthand defined in the Statement (and, for an ordinary regular patch, [F8]); if $\operatorname{div}B=0$ the middle term vanishes. We require in addition that $D$ be Jordan measurable; this is explained below and holds for every finite elementary Green region. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval and let

$$r:D\times I\to\mathbb R^3$$

be a map that extends to a $C^2$ map ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]) on an open neighbourhood of $D\times I\subseteq\mathbb R^3$. Write $p=(u,v)$ for the parameter point, write $r_u(p,t),r_v(p,t),r_t(p,t)\in\mathbb R^3$ for the partial derivatives of that $C^2$ extension at $(p,t)$, and require

$$r_u(p,t)\times r_v(p,t)\ne0\qquad\text{for every }(p,t)\in D^\circ\times I^\circ,$$

the cross product being that of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]. For every $t\in I^\circ$ this gives rank two on $D^\circ$. It does not imply the connectedness or interior injectivity required by [[def-admissible-regular-parametrized-surface-patch]]; neither is a standing hypothesis here. At endpoint or singleton times the rank condition is not imposed.

The **swept set** of the family is

$$S:=\bigcup_{t\in I}r(D\times\{t\})\subseteq\mathbb R^3,\qquad \Sigma:=\{(r(p,t),t):p\in D,\ t\in I\}\subseteq\mathbb R^4 .$$

A **velocity field for $r$** is a pair $(W,v)$ consisting of an open set $W\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ with $\Sigma\subseteq W$ and a map $v:W\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^1$ such that

$$v\bigl(r(p,t),t\bigr)=r_t(p,t)\qquad\text{for every }(p,t)\in D\times I .$$

Such a pair is required to exist: the standing hypothesis of this definition is that a velocity field for $r$ is given, and $v$ denotes it. The equality above is what single-valuedness means here: whenever two parameter points at the same time map to the same spatial point, their time derivatives agree. Values at different times may differ.

Finally let $B:V\to\mathbb R^3$ be a $C^1$ field on an open set $V\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ containing $\Sigma$. The **flux of $B$ through the patch at time $t\in I$** is

$$\Phi(t):=\int_D\bigl\langle B\bigl(r(p,t),t\bigr),\,r_u(p,t)\times r_v(p,t)\bigr\rangle\,du\,dv,$$

the integral being the Riemann integral over the compact Jordan measurable set $D$ of the displayed continuous integrand, and the pairing being the Euclidean inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. This is a parametrized flux, counted with the supplied parametrization.
